# Project Synopsis

# AI Business Manager for WhatsApp (Alaje)

# Our Solution

Most Nigerian SMEs aren't running their business on any real system, they're running it on WhatsApp, memory, an exercise book, and maybe an Excel sheet if the owner is fairly comfortable with computers. ERP systems exist that could fix this properly, but in practice they don't get adopted, because they cost too much, take too long to learn, and were built with a much bigger company in mind than a shop owner selling provisions. Our solution doesn't try to pull the owner away from WhatsApp to fix that. It works from inside it. The AI business manager sits in the same chat window the owner already uses all day, and they talk to it the same way they'd talk to an employee they trust to keep the books straight.

# How It Works

Say the owner sends "Sold 3 cartons of Indomie to Chika for ₦42,000." That one message is enough. The AI logs the sale, updates the inventory count, generates the invoice, and tells the owner where the customer's balance stands, all without them touching a form or a spreadsheet. The same chat handles inventory (stock levels, low stock warnings, tracking what's been ordered from suppliers), customer records (who's bought what, who still owes money), and reporting (daily, weekly, monthly numbers on revenue and profit, either as PDF or Excel if that's what they need for a bank or an investor).

We know typing everything out isn't realistic for most owners, so we're not requiring it. A voice note works the same as a typed message. A photo of a receipt gets read and logged as an expense. If a customer forwards an order request, that becomes a logged order and invoice without the owner retyping it. Bank alerts forwarded into the chat get matched against outstanding balances automatically. None of this depends on the owner changing how they already work, it just means the busywork gets handled for them.

The AI isn't only reactive either. If stock for a product is running low, it says so before the owner notices it's gone. If a regular customer hasn't ordered in a couple of weeks, it flags that. If the numbers suggest cash might get tight before the next supplier payment is due, it warns the owner ahead of time rather than after the fact.

# Why It Matters

We considered whether this was really any different from another to-do list app, and we don't think it is one. A to-do list still expects the owner to know what needs doing and write it down themselves. What we're building does that part for them, pulls together what's actually happening in the business, works out what needs attention first, and helps them act on it from the one app they already have open all day. We're not trying to compete with Odoo, ERPNext, or Zoho on how many features we can pack in. What we're actually up against is a paper notebook, a bad memory, and a WhatsApp chat history nobody ever goes back to read. The reason this wins isn't that it does more than those tools, it's that it doesn't ask anything new of the owner. If they can already use WhatsApp, they can already use this.

# What We Are Building

For the hackathon, we're building a working version of this: a WhatsApp assistant that handles the core of running a small business through conversation. That's recording sales and expenses, generating and tracking invoices, keeping tabs on who owes what, and managing stock with low stock alerts. Alongside that, we're building out voice note handling, receipt OCR, order creation from forwarded messages, and bank alert reconciliation, since these are what actually cut down the manual work rather than just moving it into a chat window.

# Implementation Plan (MVP)

# WhatsApp AI Business Manager: Implementation Plan

# Summary

An AI business manager reachable entirely over WhatsApp, built as an agentic system with tool access rather than a fixed set of chat commands. The owner talks to it in plain language, the agent decides which tools to call (record a sale, check a balance, generate a report), calls them, and replies with the outcome. No menus, no rigid command syntax. This is an MVP build scoped to what is feasible given the hackathon timelines.

# Core Components

| Component | Responsibility |
| :---- | :---- |
| WhatsApp channel | Inbound/outbound messaging via the Meta Cloud API, text and image only. |
| Agent orchestrator | Loop that takes an incoming message, decides which tool to call, executes it, and produces a reply. |
| Tool layer | Three tools: `record_sale`, `record_expense`, `run_report`. Each deterministic and independently testable. |
| Data store | Business, Product, and Transaction tables, all scoped by business\_id. A Business row with a null name means onboarding is in progress. |
| Media processing | OCR for receipt images only, feeding into `record_expense` the same as a typed message. |

# Data Model

| Entity | Key Fields | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Business | id, whatsapp\_number, name (nullable), created\_at | A row is created on first contact from an unmatched number with `name` null. It doubles as the onboarding state, no separate table needed. |
| Product | id, business\_id, name, stock\_qty, low\_stock\_threshold | Owner-defined at setup, or created on first mention in a sale. |
| Transaction | id, business\_id, type (sale/expense), amount, product\_ref (nullable), source (typed/ocr), created\_at | `source` distinguishes an OCR-derived expense from a typed one, useful for debugging if OCR extraction goes wrong. |
| Tool Call Log | id, business\_id, tool\_name, arguments, result, success (bool), created\_at | Minimal audit trail, cheap to add, useful if something misfires during the live demo. |

No Customer, Invoice, or Conversation State tables. Nothing in scope touches balances owed, invoicing, or multi-step confirmation, so there's nothing for them to back.

# Tool Catalog

| Tool | Arguments | Returns | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `record_sale` | product (text), quantity, amount | transaction record, plus a low-stock flag if `stock_qty` drops below `low_stock_threshold` | Commits directly on a typed message, no confirmation step. |
| `record_expense` | description, amount, vendor (optional) | transaction record | Same tool handles a typed message and an OCR-extracted receipt, `source` field is the only difference. |
| `run_report` | period (today/week) | revenue, expenses, profit for the period; week variant also returns a PDF link | Powers both the on-request revenue summary and the closing weekly report. |

# Error Handling

| Failure | Behavior |
| :---- | :---- |
| OCR fails to extract amount or vendor | Agent asks for the missing field directly, does not log an incomplete expense. |
| Tool call throws | Agent tells the owner the action didn't go through, does not claim success. Logged as `success: false`. |
| Ambiguous intent | Agent asks a clarifying question instead of guessing which tool to call. |
| LLM call fails | Retried once, then a plain "something went wrong, try again" reply. Never a silent drop. |

# Build Plan

| Area | What We're Building | How | Why It Matters |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| WhatsApp channel | Inbound/outbound messaging | Meta Cloud API webhook, signature verification, message-id dedupe. | Foundation everything else sits on, and dedupe is cheap enough to include even at MVP scope. |
| Business resolution \+ onboarding | Multi-tenant lookup with self-serve setup | Business table keyed by whatsapp\_number. Unmatched number gets a Business row created with name null and a welcome reply; the next message from that number fills in the name. No separate onboarding state table, the nullable field does the job. | Two messages gets a new business fully set up, no manual seeding needed, and it's still a small, self-contained addition. |
| Agent orchestrator | Core reasoning loop | LLM function-calling loop, one tool call per message, no chaining needed since the three tools don't depend on each other's output. | Keeps the loop simple, no need for the multi-step chaining the full plan describes. |
| `record_sale` | Sale logging \+ stock decrement | Single tool: writes a transaction, decrements `stock_qty`, checks against `low_stock_threshold`, returns the flag. | Covers demo steps 2, 3, and 6 in one tool instead of three separate ones. |
| `record_expense` | Expense logging | Single tool, called either from a typed message or from OCR output, distinguished only by the `source` field. | Same tool for both entry paths keeps the build small without losing the receipt-upload demo moment. |
| Receipt OCR | Image-to-text extraction | Image received, OCR run, extracted text handed to `record_expense` as if it were typed. | This is the one piece of "reduce manual work" functionality kept in the MVP, it's a strong demo beat for not much build time. |
| `run_report` | Revenue summary \+ weekly PDF | One tool, two period arguments, week variant also renders a PDF. | Covers both the on-request summary and the closing report moment. |
| Tool call logging | Minimal audit trail | One row per tool call, input/output/success. | Cheap insurance, if something misfires mid-demo you can see exactly what the agent tried to do. |

# Implementation Phases

| Phase | Work | Deliverable | Acceptance Criteria |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Messaging skeleton \+ business resolution \+ onboarding | Webhook in/out working, dedupe on message id, unmatched numbers walked through the two-message onboarding, resolved businesses passed to a stub tool. | A brand new number gets asked for a business name, replies with it, and immediately after can trigger the stub tool scoped to its own business\_id. Sending the same webhook payload twice produces exactly one reply. |
| 2 | `record_sale` | Sale creates a transaction, decrements stock, flags low stock in the reply. | Selling past the threshold triggers the warning in the same reply, not a separate message. |
| 3 | `run_report` (today) | Revenue summary on request. | Report numbers match the sum of the day's transactions exactly. |
| 4 | `record_expense` \+ receipt OCR | Typed expenses and OCR-derived expenses both land in the same table, OCR failures prompt for the missing field. | An unreadable receipt photo never produces a logged transaction with a missing amount. |
| 5 | `run_report` (week) \+ PDF | Weekly report with a downloadable PDF link. | PDF numbers match the report's own numbers exactly, no separate calculation path. |

# Guardrails

- The agent never writes a transaction outside the tool layer, no direct database access from the reasoning step.  
- Every tool call is logged with input, output, and success/failure.  
- The agent doesn't invent numbers. A failed or empty tool result gets reported as a failure, not papered over.  
- Webhook messages are deduped on WhatsApp's message id before reaching the agent.

# Rollout Plan

1. Messaging skeleton with dedupe and a stub tool.  
2. `record_sale` with inline low-stock warning.  
3. `run_report(today)`.  
4. `record_expense` plus receipt OCR.  
5. `run_report(week)` with PDF export.

# Notes from the WhatsApp loan channel — things to watch for building this again

Pulled from actual production shege hit while running and fixing the pecunia WhatsApp loan-origination channel (a similarly-shaped agentic WhatsApp system: agent loop, tool calling, WhatsApp Flows for structured data collection). Not a plan, just things worth being deliberate about this time.

- **Never trust the phone number as a raw string key.** WhatsApp sends inbound numbers in one format (international, no `+`); a number entered/stored elsewhere can be in local format. An exact-match lookup on `whatsapp_number` will silently miss existing businesses and treat a known customer as brand new. Normalize to variants (local/international/E.164) and match against any of them from day one — this bit us hard and was invisible until a real customer hit it.

- **Keep security/identity-resolution decisions out of the LLM's hands entirely.** Which business a message belongs to, whether a number is already linked, etc. must be resolved by deterministic server-side code before the agent loop ever sees the result — never something the model infers or decides. The model should decide *when* to act, not *whose data* it's acting on.

- **Give every terminal/error state a way back in, not just a way to die.** A conversation that hits a failure state and just gets soft-deleted/restarted from scratch forces an already-known user through onboarding again, every time. Always have a "pick this back up" path for a user who's already identified, distinct from a genuinely fresh start.

- **Cap repeated failures/off-topic churn, and don't conflate the two.** A customer who keeps getting invalid/failed responses and one who's just chatting off-topic are different situations — a tight cap on real failures (something is actually broken) and a looser cap on unproductive-but-valid turns (protects against token burn/abuse without punishing a customer asking a few real questions) served us better than one blunt counter.

- **Fact-checking a generated reply against exact string matches is brittle.** If you validate that a reply contains a specific fact (an amount, a date), normalize currency symbols, commas, decimal cents, and punctuation on both sides before comparing — otherwise a trivially-correct paraphrase gets rejected and silently swapped for a generic fallback.

- **Any code pulled from a real-world source (bank codes, product SKUs, category codes) is not guaranteed unique — don't use it as a UI element's identity.** We used a bank's real code as a WhatsApp Flow dropdown option's `id` and hit two banks sharing the same code, which broke the whole screen client-side with zero server-side error. Use your own DB row id as the client-facing identifier for anything dynamically listed, and translate back to the real value server-side when it's submitted.

- **A rich client (WhatsApp Flow, or any native UI) can fail to render a perfectly valid, schema-correct response, and there will be nothing in your logs.** The failure is entirely client-side. Don't assume "no error logged" means "nothing went wrong" — build a fast way to get real repro details (screenshot, exact screen/step) from whoever hits it, because logs alone will not show you this class of bug.

- **Don't reuse the same message copy across genuinely different flows without checking it stays true for all of them.** We had one generic "a code has been sent to your email" message used for both an actual-OTP flow and a no-OTP flow — true for one, false for the other, every time.

- **Never let an unhandled exception surface as a raw/opaque failure to the user.** A bare try/catch that returns a generic 500 (or equivalent) makes every possible root cause look identical from the outside, and some clients (WhatsApp Flow included) can't even render it, so the user just sees a dead end. Always log the real exception (message + stack + enough context to know which call threw) at the point of catch, and where possible degrade gracefully instead of going silent.

- **Static/generated config that's supposed to match what's live elsewhere (a Flow JSON schema built from your own field definitions, a synced product/definition list) can drift without anyone noticing.** Worth a way to check they still match rather than discovering it live, same as any other schema-across-two-systems problem.

- **Multi-tenant scoping (`business_id`) needs to be checked everywhere a lookup touches shared data, not assumed.** A badly-scoped query is a silent cross-tenant leak until someone finds it the hard way.

- **Plan for needing real reproduction data, not just code review, to catch the actual bugs.** More than one of the real issues here (the phone format mismatch, the duplicate bank code) were only findable by reproducing live and reading the actual data — careful code review alone missed both. Build in structured logging with enough context that a repro doesn't need a temporary debug patch to be diagnosable.
